articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Department will host an informational open house on proposed housing and the City’s Housing Element on Wednesday, November 9 from 5:00 to 6:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. Residents can learn about proposed updates to the Housing Element and timelines for submittal, certification, and implementation to the state. Piedmont city staff will seek City Council authorization to submit the City’s Draft Housing Element to the California Department of Housing & Community Development for review at a special meeting on Tuesday, November 15. On August 1, the Piedmont City Council directed city staff to analyze the viability of potential changes to the Draft Housing Element. Staff and consultants have completed the analysis and will present an inventory of revised sites. The changes include: • Increased reliance on Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) to meet State-mandated housing production targets • Relocation of affordable units in the sites inventory from the Civic Center area to the mixed-use zone on Grand Avenue • Expansion of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan area to include all city-owned property along Moraga Avenue The state deadline for cities to adopt a compliant Housing Element is January 31, 2023. Once Piedmont submits a Draft Housing Element for review, the California Department of Housing & Community has up to 90 days to return comments with requested revisions. Working to minimize any potential period of non-compliance, Planning & Building staff are in regular communication with HCD reviewers. The meeting will take place at City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, at 6 p.m. on Tuesday. November 15. articles.text: The Cain family in Wildwood Gardens received a special delivery early Saturday morning, two days before Halloween. Their son, 1st grader Timothy Cain, was the winner in guessing the weight of the 1006-pound jumbo pumpkin, the centerpiece of the Wildwood Dads Pumpkin Patch. Timothy guessed 1004 pounds, narrowly beating out the next closest guess, 1003 pounds, and more than 200 other guesses. The gourd arrived at the Cain residence at 4:00 a.m. and was dropped off on a pallet via forklift by the Fuji Melon, the supplier for this year’s patch. The delivery was due at 7:00 a.m. but, like all things Halloween, the drop off occurred in the dark of night and by surprise. When asked for his secret strategy in guessing the mass of the gourd, Cain held his cards close to the chest. Despite the prying efforts of this reporter asking if he picked it up, used a tape measure, a phone app or skills from math class Cain stated, “I just looked at it.” Wildwood dads gave fair warning to the Cains that the pumpkin had started to decompose a little early this year. Wildwood Dads Club President Adam Fishman used some quick thinking and filled up a gash in Jack with some expansion foam. All things considered, the Cains were not sure quite what to do with the pumpkin. Timothy’s brother, William, a 5th grader at Wildwood School, considered carving a jack-o-lantern face into the pumpkin with shovels. Fuji Melon agreed to return this week to cart off whatever is left of Giant Jack.

articles.text: Piedmonters will receive an Alameda County Alert at approximately 9 a.m. this Saturday, November 5, as part of the city’s first-ever wildfire evacuation drill. The drill will directly affect about 50 homes located on streets above Coaches Field off Moraga Avenue. For most residents, the alert will include instructions for an at-home wildfire readiness activity. However, residents on Maxwelton Road, Abbot Way, Echo Lane, and Nellie Avenue will receive an alert instructing them to evacuate their homes and go to Piedmont Community Hall, at 711 Highland Avenue. Emergency responders will knock on doors in this neighborhood around 9 a.m. Alerts will arrive via text and email. All residents are invited to a post-drill debriefing and preparedness event starting at 10 a.m., at Piedmont Community Hall. After remarks from city officials, participants are encouraged to ask questions and share their own experiences. The drill, which Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan conceived last spring and has been planning for the last four months, will help the readiness not only of residents but of responders as well. Because emergencies like earthquakes and wildfires can cut power lines, Brannigan is pushing for the use of walkie-talkies among responders. He also seeks to optimize communications between collaborators like the city of Oakland, Mountain View Cemetery (as an evacuation site), and the Piedmont Police Department, which is primarily responsible for organizing wildfire evacuations. The only prospective problem which Brannigan fears is low participation of local residents on account of the light rain which is forecasted on Saturday. Otherwise, in his words, “The time to have problems is during an exercise. If we have any problems, I’ll be happy about that.” “Our changing climate means wildfires are more frequent and destructive than ever,” said Brannigan. “By taking the time now to prepare our homes and practice evacuation, we will all be better prepared to take lifesaving actions quickly when a fire comes our way.” Piedmont and Alameda Counties use AC Alerts for evacuation warnings and information in the event of a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. All Piedmonters are encouraged to register for AC Alert at acalert.org, or texting their zip code to 888-777. To register in advance for the Community Hall debriefing and for information, visit piedmont. ca.gov/WildfireDrill.

articles.text: Editor: The United Nations has announced that under the current Paris agreement pledges of 166 nations, the earth is on track to warm 2.5 degree Celsius by the end of the century. Is it time to seriously consider climate engineering as a way to give more time for transitioning to clean energy? It is relatively cheap and quite effective as demonstrated by historical volcanic eruptions. Any modern nation can do it on its own without the authorization of the UN. China is likely to do it someday regardless of international opinion to avoid civil unrest and to maintain in power its harsh communist regime should the impact of warming be as bad as predicted by the climate models. Rather than worrying about “moral hazard”, let’s put this technology on the forefront of discussion and research. As an alternative to spraying sulfur aerosol in the stratosphere, could Elon Musk redirect his Mars effort towards deploying a 1000 square kilometer shield (for example as one thousand one square km shields) at the L1 Laplacian point between the sun and the earth? It would cool the earth by one degree Celsius.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. During the next several weeks and months, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pragmatists. years of the Piedmont Post every Wednesday afternoon. –Kent & Kathy Penwell generations. When you introduced yourself to me 25 years ago, we had a very compelling conversation that I had heard many times before growing up at the dinner table. You stood for open, safe communication and the integrity of a story (just like my father and grandfather). We instantly hit it off. You needed advertising and I needed a trusted venue that would continue to embrace my company’s legacy and the story of Piedmont itself. Perhaps it was selfish, but it was a terrific trade! Your insights and pushbacks are as refreshing today as 25 years ago. Your ability to run from the playing field to a night at the Symphony and every nuance in between is pretty remarkable. articles.text: Editor: We live at 1211 Oakland Avenue at the corner of Jerome. We received a public notice Saturday about a proposed bulb-out in front of our house. The bulb-out would eliminate all three parking spaces in front of our house as well as the two spaces in front of the neighboring property at 1209 Oakland Avenue. A bus stop would also be relocated in front of our house. These are very significant costs. While sharing the City Council’s commitment to safer streets, we disagree with the proposed measures to slow traffic and make crossing safer on Oakland Avenue. Recently, speed bumps were installed on Greenbank and seem to be working well. Putting speed bumps on Oakland Avenue would be significantly less expensive and disruptive than constructing eight bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections, eliminating a net of 10 parking spaces, relocating four bus stops, and removing two mature trees, as the current plans provide. Traffic lights would be another less disruptive option. We applaud the city’s commitment to making Piedmont’s streets safer. We do not agree with the proposed solution, however. There are significantly less expensive and disruptive alternatives available that do not require the destruction of mature trees. Killing trees in order to build concrete bulb-outs could not be further from the agenda of protecting nature and combating global warming. We urge the City Council to reject this over-engineered, costly, disruptive, and anti-environmental proposal. -Jonah Levy and Helga Ying
articles.title: Proposed bulb-outs not the solution to slow traffic on Oakland Ave.

articles.text: Before there was “social media” there was the Piedmont Post. Starting in 1998, the new hometown newspaper provided more than the sports scores, want ads and a few newsy items; it became a public forum for controversial items in town, providing detailed coverage (sometimes not appreciated by all) as well as unrestricted space for the residents to present their ideas, clarifications and objections. A couple of examples that come to mind are stories about undergrounding of utilities in some neighborhoods, and Measure E, the earthquake retrofitting of Piedmont schools. A good deal of the content of the paper is contributed by community members and organizations, so there are a great number of stories about the groups that are actively providing services and activities in the community. As a person actively involved in Scouting I have exhibited the Post numerous times to Scout Councils throughout the country as an example of what can be done to promote the Scout program through local papers. To date I have seen nothing anywhere that covers youth programs as well. Wes Smith is a former president of the Piedmont Scout Council, and a current member of the National Executive Committee of Boy Scouts of America.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 2, 2022 3 25th Anniversary of Piedmont Post The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. Starting in 1998, the new hometown newspaper provided more than the sports scores, want ads and a few newsy items; it became a public forum for controversial items in town, providing detailed coverage (sometimes not appreciated by all) as well as unrestricted space for the residents to present their ideas, clarifications and objections. As a person actively involved in Scouting I have exhibited the Post numerous times to Scout Councils throughout the country as an example of what can be done to promote the Scout program through local papers. To date I have seen nothing anywhere that covers youth programs as well. We received a public notice Saturday about a proposed bulb-out in front of our house. The bulb-out would eliminate all three parking spaces in front of our house as well as the two spaces in front of the neighboring property at 1209 Oakland Avenue. A bus stop would also be relocated in front of our house. These are very significant costs. While sharing the City Council’s commitment to safer streets, we disagree with the proposed measures to slow traffic and make crossing safer on Oakland Avenue. Recently, speed bumps were installed on Greenbank and seem to be working well. Putting speed bumps on Oakland Avenue would be significantly less expensive and disruptive than constructing eight bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections, eliminating a net of 10 parking spaces, relocating four bus stops, and removing two mature trees, as the current plans provide. Traffic lights would be another less disruptive option. We applaud the city’s commitment to making Piedmont’s streets safer. We do not agree with the proposed solution, however. There are significantly less expensive and disruptive alternatives available that do not require the destruction of mature trees. Killing trees in order to build concrete bulb-outs could not be further from the agenda of protecting nature and combating global warming. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion today on the invasion of Ukraine by Russia. The guest speaker is Steven Pifer, Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine. The discussion will be held on Zoom at 5 p.m., Wednesday, November 2. The war in Ukraine is the largest land war since World War II. Listen to the latest about the current situation from a diplomatic, military, and economic viewpoint, as well as possible trajectories for the war. Ambassador Pifer will address implications for international security, not only for Ukraine and Russia but also for the US and the EU. Ambassador Pifer is an affiliate with the Center for International Security and Cooperation at Stanford and a nonresident senior fellow with the Brookings Institution. A retired Foreign Service officer, in a career of more than 25 years with the Department of State, he served as deputy assistant secretary with responsibilities for Russia and Ukraine, U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, and special assistant to the President and senior director for Russia, Ukraine and Eurasia on the National Security Council. He also served at the U.S. embassies in Warsaw, Moscow and London as well as with the U.S. delegation to the negotiation on intermediate-range nuclear forces in Geneva. articles.text: The 21st Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot will be the same family-friendly race with a step or two towards a greener footprint. As the 5K race tries to find ways to minimize the impact on the planet and keep within the City of Piedmont guidelines, this year’s Turkey Trot is saving material resources by using smaller sized race bibs. The bibs are half the size and twice the value. Some people save their race bibs but the majority do not. They wind up as landfill waste. Race bibs will be collected after this year’s race to send to a recycling program along with the pins for future reuse. articles.text: Final of an 8-part series The Post wraps up its election preview series this week. With the election just days away residents are now entrusted to do their civic duty by voting by November 8. Piedmont is always at the top of voter turnout in Alameda County, and among the highest in the state. The Post thanks all candidates City Council and School Board for their willingness to answer questions each week for a period of two months. Every week, two questions are sent out on Thursday and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to 150 words per question. City Council 3 open seats, 6 candidates. Week 8 QUESTIONS 1. If elected, what is on your short list of what you hope to accomplish in the first two years? 2. This is the last week of questions from the Post prior to the November 8 election. Do you have any final comments? JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. Accomplish in First Two Years If elected, my first two years will be focused on helping to select our next City Administrator, bringing critical infrastructure projects like the pool and dispatch center to fruition, further developing a vision for our City’s growth, and creating a robust community engagement process outside of chambers. 2. Final Comments As a current member of the Council it has been a privilege to serve. Over the course of my campaign I have had the opportunity to get to know our community better and to hear about issues that concern our residents. This campaign has only strengthened my commitment to continue in my role, should I be fortunate enough to be elected. I would like to thank the Piedmont Post, my fellow candidates, and the Piedmont community for the part each has played in making this a positive and informative campaign season. On November 8th, please make your voices heard. Think of our city as a tiny nation. We are 1,000 acres, the same size as Central Park. Love your neighbour as you do yourself, visit the sick and the prisoners. Protect the animals and the babies and children and elderly in particular. delayed their Housing Element. The State also accelerated the timeline to complete Santa Monica’s updated design guidelines, taking away even more local control from the city. Let’s work together and avoid a costly fight with the State. Let’s also complete our due diligence process and create a detailed facilities condition assessment report of our civic buildings outlining options and costs for repair/replacement or a combination of both to protect our critical facilities. 2. Final Comments Thank you to the Post for providing this weekly Q&A forum throughout the campaign and it’s also worth recognizing (and appreciating) that politics in Piedmont have a different tone than what is considered the “norm” these days on the national stage. So, thank you to all the candidates and all our neighbors for being involved, being respectful, and voting! This experience gives me one more reason why I think Piedmont is a great town. Feel free to contact me at tom@ vote4tomramsey.com JEANNE SOLNORDAL 1. Accomplish in First Two Years My two-year short list is as follows: • Submit a resident approved version of the Housing Element plan. I support a vote before any rezoning. • Obtain pool bids that meet the needs, not desires, of Piedmont residents. Over building and excess costs need to be avoided. It is my experience that Piedmont tends to be overcharged by contractors. Costs should be carefully compared to those being charged in other cities. • Getting design reviews completed for the infrastructure needs at the Civic Center is critical. Time is of the essence to avoid inflated costs. • Assess school and park crosswalk safety. Safer crossings are needed to avert potential dangers to our youth. • Work with the administrators at the PUSD to ensure our excellent test scores are sustained. • Connect with the Climate Action team to re-promote the rideshare to work program. • Establish two EV charging stations centrally located in City Center. 2. Final Comments I want to thank all residents for taking the time to listen to many candidates. Being involved in politics, I understand the enormous amount of campaign materials received daily. An important fact to remember: in 1868 the Fourteenth amendment established equal protections for all citizens. In 1870 the Fifteenth amendment ratified that all citizens regardless of race, origin, etc. had the right to vote. Our state constitution also grants us this right. The Piedmont City Charter specifically gives residents the right to vote on rezoning changes. Voting is such an important right that any attempt, by anyone, to circumvent that right should be met with great skepticism and scrutiny. Demand your right to vote on all rezoning changes. Circumventing voting rights sets our history back more than a century. This is digressive not progressive. Many thanks to Jay Russell at Piedmont Post for providing this platform to candidates. Our crime rate was escalating so I promoted cameras at every entrance [to the city] and augmenting license plate readers. articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.

articles.text: Michael Malione ALPS (Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students) is a parent support group that advocates for more solid academics at PUSD and provides families with resources and opportunities to engage their children in deeper and more joyful learning. The group has been gaining steam and making impactful strides in advancing academic focus in the community. As the 2022 school board election race comes to a close, we wish to remind the community that as a parent support organization, we cannot directly endorse candidates. Our members and officers have, as individuals, taken a variety of positions on matters relating to the current state of academics at PUSD and the school board candidates. We firmly believe that strong academics and DEIB improvements can and should coexist to help all children reach their full potential while making the world a better place for all. While in theory the school district can achieve both, in practice there are people in PUSD who’ve proffered an unbalanced approach that undermines students’ academic potential. All three candidates for school board care strongly about academics. We hold that it is critical to select high-quality curricula and provide the right professional development opportunities for our teachers. Given that more than 30% of PUSD students are high-performing, we consider the guidance from the state of California to be a floor, not the ceiling for our district. Our district has in recent years lurched in directions that are not in sync with the great expertise that exists among the various sectors of our community—teachers, professionals, and parents alike. We urge you to vote for candidates whom you think will be able to stand up to the administration and advocate for the needs of our children. Parent Sharing Forum We held our first Parent Sharing Forum in October. It was a chance to welcome new parents, and how to get the most from differentiated instruction, early reading and mathematics. Registration will soon be opening for the longest-standing enrichment program, Math Kangaroo, an international competition for grades 1 to 12 that focuses on problem-solving. We will host a virtual Q&A session about it on Monday, November 14 at 8 pm. We also offer Learning Circles, which we’ll be promoting in advance of the next session. Many of our officers and board members participated in both special school board meetings, to provide feedback on the drafted mission and vision statements. They’ve expressed that the district’s mission should include academic focus and opportunities for each child to reach their full potential. We had a productive discussion with Dr. Evans about education at PUSD and academic rigor in our schools. We welcome his bold support for improving the differentiated instruction and academic curriculum throughout PUSD. With exciting work happening in the district on literacy and rewriting its mission and vision, there is increased optimism that academics will once again become a priority. To get the latest information about ALPS programs and opportunities, visit the Piedmont Store (piedmontstore. org), and click on Parent Support Groups. Ella Grossberg and Michael Malione are co-Presidents of Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students.

articles.text: ASB and Affinity Mentorship Class host forum on campus Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Eleven students from ASB and the Affinity Mentorship Class hosted a forum for all three school board candidates on October 28 in the new Alan Harvey Theater Sohrab “Seb” Ford Members of the high school student government (ASB) and the Affinity Mentorship Class hosted a panel discussion for the three candidates running for Piedmont School Board on Friday, October 28 in the new Alan Harvey Theater. Each student on the questioning panel asked a question and each of the three candidates had 90 seconds to answer. The candidates were Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson and Shirley Hooi. Although few students at PHS are age 18 and eligible to vote, the forum is the first to date of any Piedmont Candidates that has been held in person. Although attendance was optional for the 10:15 a.m. forum, students, teachers and administrators filled the theater. “It’s important that students become aware and involved in local elections like the school board because they directly impact our day to day lives, more then they impact anyone else. Students need to get their voices heard.” said Ruby Guzdar after the event. With the theater’s wifi not working, the forum felt like an old-time town hall meeting with speakers relying on the strength of their voices to be heard. Students on the questioning panel included student board member Cleo Tahawi, Junior Class President Jack Cramer, Ruby Guzdar, Elena Stevens, Inaya Majid, and Meher Bachher. Medhekar answered a question about discrimination by saying, “There is a debate between diversity and academics that’s been going on. And I think that it’s just not either/ or,” she said. “I think that one thing that the district is not doing well is talking about incidents that happen, we have to respect students privacy, but we need to also talk about what is happening,” Medhekar added. In response to a question over a controversial curriculum, Hooi suggested providing multiple options to students and parents in order to let them decide which readings and opinions they felt were most important. Thomasson emphasized the importance of opening up discussion between students and board members, Thomasson suggested re-implementing “school board listening sessions” or “office hours” that the school held during the pandemic shelter-in-place order. The Affinity Mentorship program began in 2020 and in 2022 was recognized as a class in the 8th period. The year-long course currently has 33 students. Mentors offer sessions to elementary and middle school students of similar affinities in order to explore and learn about themselves and their identities. Piedmont residents will go to the polls on Tuesday, November 8 to select two of the three candidates to join the school board. Photo by Jay Russell The lower section of the theater was filled with students to hear from school board candidates vying for two seats.

The sun will go down and finally, he will leave. The trees, the birds and the stars watch him. He doesn’t notice, he’s hunched over. It is dark, he doesn’t see the path in front of him. He knows he doesn’t need to; he has walked the path many times and knows where it leads. It ends at the playground where he sits on a swing and lights his pipe. He pulls his coat tighter around his aging body. Only the embers of his tobacco are seen in the dark night, momentarily reflecting his sunken face and faded blue eyes. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: The Highlander boys’ water polo team swept through the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament at San Leandro High on its way to a second consecutive league title, defeating San Leandro in the opening round 20-3 on Tuesday, October 25, Lick-Wilmerding 11-6 in the semifinals on October 27, and s 13-4 drubbing in the finals on Saturday, October 29. PHS was undefeated and the clear favorite entering the post-season playoffs. Last year Piedmont narrowly defeated No. 1 Berkeley 12-8. “This is a testament to the kids coming and working every single day, the leadership we had from our juniors and seniors, and the way they grew into the program,” said assistant coach John Savage, who stepped aside from the lead role after being head coach for the previous nine years. Piedmont was able to lean on its defense against Alameda, and allowed no goals until the third quarter. Goalie Dariush Kashani had 15 saves, and the PHS defenders forcing the Hornets to attempt scoring from long range. “It all comes down to defense; that’s what we stressed the most. We have the best goalie in the league, but it comes down to team defense. We run press defense and then we run a drop, which basically forces players to cover 2-3 guys at once. It’s really a team effort, and that’s what’s really carried us through the season,” said head coach Rik Krumins. “These guys keep me on my toes. We all work hard and get the job done. I’d like to highlight our chemistry, we worked very well together. We executed well in the second half. Quincy Scherman did great coming back on defense, same for Finn Burke,” said Kashani. Much of this year’s team contributed on 2021’s league title as well, but the Highlanders entered the league tournament as the No. 3 seed last time around. This time, the postgame celebration was a bit more subdued with the Highlanders, far and away the better side. Staff Photos Goalie Dariush Kashani had 15 saves in the finals against the Hornets. Peter Krumins led the rout of Alameda with six goals – a double hat trick. Piedmont water pollo players and coaches with their second consecutive WACC Championship banner after defeating Alameda 13-4 in the finals. “Last year, we focused on shutting down one guy for Berkeley. Now, coming into this game, we were the No. 1 team. It felt a lot different. Our practices were much more like swim-team practices. We’ve been countering and you wouldn’t see us counter like that last year. We’re in a lot better shape,” said Peter Krumins, who led the team in scoring with six goals. “We flipped the script this year,” added Declan Linnane. “We weren’t supposed to win it last year; we were the underdogs. This year, we had a dominant league season and we just continued that to the championship game,” Piedmont will enter the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs on Saturday, November 5. as the No. 3 seed and a first-round bye. 13-4 win over Alameda In the first quarter, PHS was first on the board when Krumins assisted George Stein 40 seconds into the match. However, Alameda tied one minute later. The Hornets had an opportunity to take the lead with a 5-meter penalty shot at the 4:46 mark, but Kashani came through with a big save. From there, Piedmont recorded eight shot attempts, which included throws by Krumins and Stein hitting the crossbar. The second quarter started with Kashani stopping three shots in the first two minutes of action, leading to Krumins scoring at 5:13 to give Piedmont the lead. Stein scored 30 seconds later to put PHS ahead 3-1, while Stein assisted Krumins at 3:22 to make it 4-1. In the remaining time, Alameda scored twice but Kashani had two saves, including a big stop on a breakaway opportunity. In the third, Piedmont scored five unanswered goals to put the match out of reach at 9-3. Krumins assisted Farris Saffouri 45 seconds into the quarter, followed by Linnane drawing a 5-meter penalty 30 seconds later, enabling Krumins to score. Krumins scored again with 3:33 to go, while Linnane assisted Krumins at the two-minute mark. Stein scored once more with 10 seconds on the block. Daniel Banin scored in the fourth quarter to make it 10-3 with 5:15 to play, while Krumins assisted Quincy Scherman 45 seconds later. Finn Burke then scored on another assist by Krumins with 3:55 remaining. Alameda scored its first goal of the second half with 3:05 on the clock and added one more at 1:45 with Piedmont rotating bench players in. Krumins scored the final goal of the match at 1:32. Final stats: Krumins had six goals and two assists. Stein had three goals, an assist and steal. Burke, Saffouri, and Scherman had individual goals. Kashani had 15 saves and two steals. 11-6 win over Lick-Wilmerding PHS led 5-1 by the end of the first quarter and 7-3 by halftime. It scored two goals and allowed one in the third period to lead 9-4 before scoring twice in the fourth period, 11-6. Final stats: Linnane had three goals, an assist and a steal. Krumins scored three and had an assist. Saffouri had two goals and a steal. Burke had two goals. Stein had a goal and a steal. Kashani had nine saves. 20-3 win over San Leandro Piedmont led comfortably 7-0 by the end of the first quarter and 10-0 by halftime. It extended the gap to 14-1 in the third and closed out with six more goals in the fourth. PHS finished with 10 different goal scorers. Final stats: Hayden Jahn had four goals and two steals. Elles Krieckhaus had four goals, an assist and steal. Burke and Banin had two goals. Stein had two goals, an assist, and steal. Leo Hurwitz had two goals, an assist, and four steals. Evan Dickason had a goal and two assists. Spencer Barlow had a goal, assist, and steal. Scherman scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (19-6 overall, 9-0 league) play the winner of No. 6 Novato and No. 11 Lick-Wilmerding on Saturday, November 5. Location and start time is To Be Determined.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team return to its tradition of winning every match every year. Last week it defeated Berkeley 4-3 at home on Tuesday, October 25, and rolled over Bishop O’Dowd 6-1 at Merritt College on Thursday, October 27. It was the team’s first league title since 2018. In the process, the Highlanders were a perfect 12-0 against WACC schools, something they achieved for 19 consecutive years between 2000-2018. It was the third win of the season against O’Dowd after defeating the Dragons 4-3 on October 11 and 5-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno in September. This time, BOD was without two players, which forced them to pack their No. 1 doubles team with their usual top-two singles starters. Piedmont’s clinching fourth victory on match day was at No. 2 doubles with Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon winning 6-4, 6-2. “To be honest, I was kind of expecting us to win the title. We’ve beaten O’Dowd before and I knew we could do it again. Our Emma Eisemon (front) and Cecilia DeFazio captured the clinching win against Bishop O’Dowd to solidify Piedmont’s undefeated league championship season. Photo by Jacque Jumper Piedmont honored its five seniors on the roster on October 25 against Berkeley. Pictured are: Sophia Kalamas (left), Anne Jumper, Mara LaForte, Talia Blumberg, and Michaela Bini. team is really strong this year,” said DeFazio, a junior. She and Eisemon were a breakout doubles team last year, and this year they are even better. “As a doubles partner, I feel like we’re a lot closer now. I think we have a better mentality this season and we come back stronger. Because we’re so close as a team and we’re so eager to win, it pushes us through our wins. With the title, it proves that we earned everything we worked towards,” said sophomore teammate Emma Eisemon. Piedmont the WACC Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 4-5, where they will compete with two singles starters and two doubles teams. 6-1 win over O’Dowd Against Bishop O’Dowd, Anne Jumper at No. 2 singles was the first win on the day, cruising to a 6-1, 6-3 victory. Quickly following was Carolina Romanczuk winning easily 6-0, 6-0 at No. 3 singles. No. 1 doubles Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini lost 6-4, 6-2 as the third match to close on the day, but soon after, Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum at No. 3 doubles won 6-4, 6-1. Eisemon and DeFazio then reeled in the clinching victory at No. 2 doubles, 6-4, 6-2. Finishing the day was Anika Gilliland winning in three sets at No. 4 singles 6-4, 3-6, 10-8, while No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova won comfortably 6-3, 6-0. 4-3 win over Berkeley Piedmont defeated Berkeley 4-3 on October 25 and took time to honor their five seniors: LaForte, Bini, Anne Jumper, Sophia Kalamas, and Talia Blumberg. PHS won all three doubles matches and the No.1. singles match. Playing in her usual spot as No. 1 singles, Kononova won 6-1, 6-0 at No. 1. Anne Jumper lost in three sets at No. 2, 6-2, 4-6, 10-3. Romanczuk fell 6-2, 6-3 at No. 3, and Gilliland lost in three sets at No. 4, 6-3, 6-7 (8-6), 6-2. In doubles, LaForte and Bini won 6-3, 7-5 at No. 1. Eisemon and DeFazio cruised 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2. Kate Jumper and Kortum won 6-1, 6-2 at No. 3. articles.text: Piedmont High football fans got a preview on Thursday, October 27 of what they can expect in the future from Piedmont’s football program after its Junior Varsity team routed Tennyson 34-0 in Hayward. It was the second consecutive decisive win for Piedmont’s JV team after thrashing St. Patrick 41-12 on October 21. Tennyson got the first possession of the game and the Lancers drove all the way to Piedmont’s 30-yard line. However, a costly penalty helped the Highlanders force a turnover on downs. Although the first quarter ended scoreless, Piedmont drove downfield with a mix of runs by sophomores Tommy Ashton, Brandon Dickie and Miles Silver, and freshman Cash Panico, to go along with sophomore quarterback Vince Arbit completing a pass to receiver Sam Shelby. Ashton put Piedmont on the scoreboard with a one yard touchdown run to break the deadlock and a 6-0 lead. PHS missed the extra point attempt. On Tennyson’s next possession, sophomore linebacker Cash Elmquist made a sensational onehanded interception and took it all the way to the end zone for a pick-six. Ashton made the twopoint conversion for a 14-0 lead. Freshman Marius Arno recovered a Lancer fumble on its next possession deep on Tennyson’s side of the field. Shortly after, Ashton sprang loose for a 17-yard TD run. Freshman Ryan Riddell converted the extra point attempt for 21-0 to end the first half. The second half started with a bang when sophomore receiver and defensive back Miguel Long took the opening kickoff all the way to the Tennyson 35-yard line. Sophomore quarterback Markos Lagios followed with a 17- yard touchdown pass to freshman Dash Waters Worthen and a 27-0 lead. In the fourth quarter, Tennyson drove to the Piedmont 20-yard line, but the defense Tommy Ashton had a pair of touchdown carries against the Lancers. made a big stop with help from sophomores Jordan Alemania, Nick King, and Logan McGilloway, as well as freshmen Adan Sotelo, Adrian Kondakov, George Bishop, and Jason Shum. Not finished for the night, the Highlanders started another drive with a 25-yard run by Ashton, and then back-to-back completions from Lagios to freshman tight end Albert capped by a 21-yard touchdown pass on a post route to make it 34-0. The winning streak gives Piedmont momentum going into the season finale on Thursday, November 3 against Kennedy of Richmond at Witter Field at 6:00 p.m. Prior to the game, PHS will honor the nine seniors on the varsity team, Jack Nelson, Ryan McConathy, Matteo and Bautista Costa, Liam Campbell, Marcos Filho, Luka Rivas Cate, Bailey Cain, and Aidan Hickman. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-3) hosts Kennedy at Witter Field on Thursday, November 3 at 6:00 p.m. with senior night festivities starting at 5:30 p.m. Markos Lagios (4) had two touchdown passes on Tennyson.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ water polo players celebrate following the game-winning goal to capture fifth-place at the WACC Tournament. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team concluded its season with a fifth-place finish in the WACC Tournament at San Leandro HS. They opened with a 13-5 loss to Castro Valley on Tuesday, October 25 but followed with a big 19-4 win over Lick-Wilmerding on Thursday, October 27. In the battle for fifth-place on Saturday, October 29, the game went into double overtime before PHS topped Berkeley 13-12 in sudden death. Katarina Melian scored the golden goal 49 seconds into the period. “In the last overtime period, and my thought going in was, ‘If I get the ball, I’m shooting.’ When they passed it down to Julia [Montes], I called for the ball and then the ball worked to Annika [Nilsson], then she passed it to me. I saw space between my defender and I knew it was the time to shoot it,” said Melian of the game-winner. It was a big game for goalie Friedie Schickedanz in Saturday’s match against the Yellowjackets, recording 11 saves on the day including three pivotal stops in overtime. “Starting out, they were shooting a lot of lobs, which have been difficult for me. They scored a bunch early, but I try to reset mentally every quarter. We switched our defense and it worked well. That helped me dial in for the rest of the game,” said Schickedanz. PHS had to battle back from a 4-1 deficit at the end of the first quarter and 7-5 disadvantage to start the fourth. “I think the main thing that brought us the win was our teamwork and our spirit. Even when we were down, everyone kept playing hard and no one gave up. We worked really well as a team just communicating,” said Melian. Piedmont concludes its season with an 8-11 overall record and watches seniors like Rosie Feldman, Odessa Dando, Annika Nilsson, Macie Gard, and Molly Ashton depart. PHS will have considerable players returning like leading scorer Melian, Schickedanz in goal, Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Kate Keyjes, Vivian Burke, Sydney Olson, Julia Montes, Sage Gilbert, and Alicia Bernales. 13-12 over Berkeley Gard scored the first goal of the game after just 15 seconds in the first quarter, but Berkeley went on to score four unanswered goals to lead 4-1 to start the second. In the second, Melian scored the second goal 30 seconds into the quarter. After a save by Schickedanz, Nilsson assisted Melian for a goal at 5:16. Berkeley then scored with 4:51 to go and the two sides traded possessions, including two saves by Schickedanz before #7 assisted Melian for a goal at 2:21. With just four seconds left in the half Melian scored again to make it 5-5 going at halftime. In the third quarter, Berkeley scored twice at the 4:10 and 3:07 marks to jump ahead 7-5 while PHS was unable to get on the board. The Yellowjackets scored two more unanswered goals in the fourth quarter to lead 9-5 with 6:13 to play, but that’s when the comeback started. From there, Gard scored on an assist by Nilsson with five minutes on the clock. After two minutes, Melian scored on a rocket from distance to make it 9-7. articles.text: Piedmont team now accepting new riders In the spirit of building community, Piedmont Mountain Bike Team recently gave four of its older loaner bikes to Skyline High School in an effort to help invigorate the Oakland school’s new program. “We have many riders of color who needed bikes in the Skyline High School bike club this year. We’re thrilled to partner with the Piedmont team and give new life to these bikes. We’re getting our program off the ground and it was great to get support from an established team,” said Skyline HS head coach Jen Ryden. In addition, the co-ed Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is currently recruiting new riders for the upcoming spring season. The team practices on local trails and competes in the spring semester against other East Bay high schools in the Norcal Mountain Bike League between December and May. Piedmont MTB has two “Fun Rides” planned in the upcoming weeks at Oakland’s Joaquin Miller Park on two consecutive Sundays, November 6 and November 13. Rides are designed to be inclusive and open to anyone. There are no registration requirements prior to the start of the racing season. Interested riders can email Piedmont MTB at Piedmontbiking@gmail.com. For more information, visit www.piedmontmtb. com. Jonathan Carmona, Skyline High School junior riding a bike donated ny the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. Piedmont’s Jasper Schuetz competes in an earlier race.

articles.text: November is here, which means Turkey day is right around the corner! If you are planning to do the Piedmont Turkey Trot, it’s time to really lace up those shoes and get in some runs before the big race on Thanksgiving morning. This week, plan to run two days of easy running using the walk/run approach and then add in a hill workout. This hill workout is specific for the last .2 mile of the race, a very sneaky hill placed right before the finish line. Do a short warm up jog (5-10 minutes) over to the Magnolia Ave and Hillside Ave intersection. Once you feel nice and warmed up, run up Magnolia Ave to Highland at a speedy pace, stop and walk back down the hill. You will repeat this a total of four times. These should be all-out sprints, as hard as you can run without stopping. This is a good time to start visualizing race day and how good it will feel to finish fast up that last stretch of the course on race day. Staff photo More than 2200 runners sped down Highland Avenue on Thanksgiving morning 2021 at the start of the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a 5-kilometer run along city streets. WEEK DAY WORKOUT November 7 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 6x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x Wednesday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 4 x run up Magnolia Ave (Start at Hillside, run to Highland) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down

articles.text: Piedmont High sophomore Mei Assalian had a strong performance at the 2022 North Coast Section championship tournament on Monday, October 24 at the Rooster Run Golf Club in Petaluma, finishing 30th of 120 golfers with an 18-hole round of 92 strokes. “Mei earning her way to NCS should be exalted around school and in the community. Mei’s a player, the moment is never too big for her,” said coach Howard Oliver proudly. “She enjoys the game for the right reasons. In reaching NCS, she sees what she can aspire to if she chooses.” Assalian, a sophomore standout, was named a team captain before the start of the season and frequently was the team’s low medalist. She qualified for the prestigious tournament by finishing eighth at the WACC Tournament at Monarch Bay on Monday, October 17. The Rooster Run course is characterized by long fairways on a collection of par-four and par-five holes, along with difficult greens that are fast and sloping, Assalian had a solid round off of the tee to hit the fairways and focused on having a productive approach on the greens. “I try to play safe, straight shots. Most of my play off of the tee got onto the fairway… One thing that was really challenging were the greens due to the slopes, so even the short puts were really difficult,” said Assalian. Mei Assalian finished with an 18-hole score of 92 strokes at NCS. Mei Assalian, a sophomore, finished 30th of 120 at the North Coast Section Championship Tournament at Rooster Run Golf Club in Petaluma. She was able to convert a birdie opportunity on the par-four 16th hole, using an eight iron on her approach shot. “One of my better holes was on the 16th. I hit a good drive and used my eight iron to get onto the green,” described Assalian. To prepare for the tournament, Assalian traveled to Petaluma one day early to get a feel of what was ahead of her. “My dad and I played there the day before. I got to know the course; I didn’t know anything about it before, so it helped me understand the angles to take and how to approach different holes,” said Assalian. League Tournament As for her day at the WACC Tournament, Piedmont competed at Monarch Bay on multiple occasions throughout the season, giving her a good familiarity with the course. They played two rounds on the nine-hole course, where she shot a collective score of 74. “We played the course twice. I think playing it the second time went a lot better, I shot a 40 and then a 34. I think going over the second time helped with my tee shots and knowing what to do,” said Assalian. “I feel like I know how to visualize better, I think that helped me a lot. After a bad hole, I began visualizing how to do better shots. I just need to keep getting out and playing,” said Assalian.

articles.text: Rugby. Fast paced, muddy, physical. Great long-sleeve shirts. A ball that resembles an American football but is bigger, and is thrown backwards. The kind of sport that builds physical strength and character in men and women the world over. You may think about countries like England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, South Africa, France, New Zealand, Samoa, Australia, as the centers of the sport. With its growing popularity in America and in Northern California, rugby is one of the fastest growing youth, amateur and professional sports. It attracts thousands of kids and young adults from middle school through high school, college and beyond. No regional youth rugby club demonstrates this growing trend toward the high energy sport more than Lamorinda Rugby Club, drawing players from throughout the East Bay. The sport is becoming so popular that the U.S. has won the bid to host the Men’s 2031 World Cup and the Women’s 2033 World Cup, gaining support from President Biden in April 2022 and winning the bid in May from the World Rugby governing body. This is an exciting time for the sport. Two of America’s leading universities offering college level rugby for both men and women are both local – St Mary’s College in Moraga and University of California in Berkeley. The current Division 1A rankings for men’s rugby in 2021 had Cal Berkeley at #1 and St Mary’s at #2. The Lamorinda Rugby Club has a long history in the area. The program started in 1980 by Pat Vincent, a former captain of the New Zealand All Blacks rugby team, first as a high-school-only team through 2001. Then, due to Tommy Ashton is one of the Piedmont players with the Lamorinda Rugby Club. the demand in the area, and the need to prepare young athletes to compete at a high level, teams of younger players were formed. The Lamorinda Rugby club now has teams for boys and girls starting at the U8 level. High School Director of Rugby Tom Lee says, “Touring and travelling as a rugby team provides some amazing benefits for the players. Obviously, team-bonding and camaraderie, but it also provides skills for life: commitment, leadership and self-reliance. Above all, though, it’s fun.” This season, the high school boys team plans to travel to Portugal and Spain during Spring Break to compete in a youth tournament with teams from Europe. The resumption of international travel after two years of lockdown due to Covid means rugby life is returning to normal. Registration for the 2022-2023 season is underway. More information can be found at https:// lamorugby.sportngin.com/register/form/625128496 Check out the Club’s “Open Days,” a great opportunity for experienced players to continue developing their skills and for new players to try out the sport. Open Days are scheduled for November 5, 12 and 19 from 10 a.m. to 12 noon at the Orinda Sports Field. Those interested can contact admin@lamorugby. com for details.

articles.text: Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) opens its 18th season with Matilda the Musical, with performances November 4–13 at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts in downtown Oakland. articles.text: Review by Jaime Robles In front of the stage’s black curtain a man rings a bell. He continues to ring, calling onto the stage 10 dancers, similarly dressed in black. Then the curtain opens and the dancers cluster, seething darkly into groups, only their faces, bare feet, hands and arms reflecting the dim light of Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Thus begins Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan’s performance, the second of Cal Performances’ dance programs for the 2022–23 season. The program, 13 Tongues, was choreographed by the company’s current artistic director, Tsung-lung Cheng. Cheng took his inspiration from the neighborhood where he grew up, Bangha, Wanhua, in Taipei. There he sold slippers as a child, navigating the chaotic streets of Taipei’s oldest district. Cloud Gate Dance Theatre, which began in 1973 under the direction of choreographer Hwaimin Lin, takes its name from the oldest dance form known in China, but the company was the first modern dance company in Taiwan and Asia. As contemporary dance, the group’s choreography is firmly based in Asian movement, both the indigenous forms of dance and martial arts. And, as the opening bell-ringing suggested, there is much of mediation and worship in their dance. There are also suggestions of ballet and Western modern dance, but the spirit of Asian movement predominates and energizes. Although Giong Lim’s electronic music accompanies much of “13 Tongues,” the music is primarily made by the dancers as they stomp, yell, scream and vocalize. Occasionally folk songs break through, melodic and choral, or the hum of Taoist chants. The use of the dancers’ voices reminded me of Jackie Chan fight scenes. Chan’s tightly choreographed fights are full of groans, cries and shouts. Though it sounds simply like random noises, the grunts and groans are a language, telling the fighters where each of them is, how close they are and what move will be made next. It’s fair to say that 13 Tongues is similar in visual effect as well. The dance is built around chaos, its unloosening and its reigning in. Chaos to order, order to chaos, chaos to order. There are comic moments and terrifying ones. These transitions are also notable in the use of color. The performance begins in darkness, with the dancers dressed in black tunics and baggy black pants, a few exposed bare arms here and there. The skin of faces and bare feet and hands becomes brighter as the lighting increases. Only the energy of the dancers’ bodies and their emphatic cries draws in the viewer. With the slow entrance of abstract green projections on the upstage scrim, the world of 13 Tongues takes on color, moving toward the bright and geometric, and more clearly defining the dancers. Then the goddess appears among them, dressed in bright fluorescent colors. She is exalted, the black-clad dancers lifting her upwards, and seemingly she floats across the stage. She removes her robes, and they are coveted by everyone, taking on a life of their own. Eventually everyone is covered in bright fluorescent colors. And the luminous skin of bare hands, feet and faces is increased by a bare chest here and there wrapped and accented by pinks, greens, yellows and reds. But these colors are oddly subterranean. The use of blacklight to set the colors glowing in the dark gives a slightly psychedelic spin to the dance, as if these figures were threads escaping from the obscure brocade of the collective unconscious. Special kudos to projections designer Ethan Wang. In the midst of this landscape of dynamic movement an enormous orange and silver koi languidly swam across the surfaces of the stage, passing through and over the clusters of black figures. The designers wisely chose to end the piece with the fish reappearing for a final lap across the stage, calmly swimming upward toward the heavens. Coming soon Cal Performances’ next dance performance is by New York– based choreographer, dancer and director Camille A. Brown, who returns with ink, the final installment of her dance trilogy on December 14-16. For information and tickets, visit calperformances.org.
articles.title: Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan comes to Berkeley

articles.text: Revelations of the liquid kind. Are you a gourmet or a gourmand? Most of us enjoy good food. That is the gourmand in us. But there is more to life than just eating well. This was clearly demonstrated to me a few years ago when I was invited to a banquet. It was a multi-course affair with every plate selected with great care. Each course was paired with a wine designed to bring out the best. All of the diners were advised to take a bite of the first course and then sip the accompanying wine. The flavor literally exploded in our mouths. What a revelation it was. Just recently I attended a class on the enjoyment of wine. The expert told us that it is better not to drink the wine but to enjoy it in other ways. He suggested that we conjure up a vocabulary to describe the wines. In wine appreciation the nose is the best sense we have, followed by the taste buds. Our instructor told us that there are no taste buds in the throat, so don’t swallow the wine. The eyes play an important part also. The first wine we sampled was from Hungary. The person next to me was a Hungarian, who observed that the wine had the color of Tokay. Soon after that, our instructor said the very same thing. The next thing we were told to do was to use our nose to breathe the wine in deeply and conjure up descriptive words. My uneducated pallet sensed citrus overtones. I was right. Our instructor used the word “linden” which is the German word for lime. A person nearby was a recovering alcoholic, but he was an enthusiastic participant. He sniffed every wine, but the wine did not touch his lips… Ever. A sensational discovery Almost 100 years ago the tomb of king Tut was discovered by Howard Carter. The date was November 4, 1922. The discovery spawned every sort of Egyptology. You can get yourself in the mood by listening to Ballet Egyptian by Luigini, selections from Aida, or Africa by St-Saens. Chamber music at Piedmont Center for the Arts The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco presented its 10th anniversary concert in Piedmont on Sunday afternoon. They showcased one of the pieces they played in their very first concert in 2012, the monumental Beethoven String Quartet Op. 132. But there were other musical pieces to admire. To begin the concert, the quartet performed a new composition by Carolyn Shaw entitled Valencia. The composer has a unique way of looking at things. Her composition was about the Valencia orange not the city in Spain. It embraced every aspect of the orange from planting to eating. It was colorful, flavorful, piquant, with zesty eruptions of juicy chords. There was even a dark section where I envisioned a chef broiling the orange. Mozart’s unique “Dissonant” quartet came next, and then the Beethoven quartet brought the concert to a conclusion. The chamber music Society of San Francisco plays with incredible technical bravado. It can become intoxicating in its perfection. Their ensemble is tight. The word “perfection” comes to mind as I listened in amazement. But then I began to think that in the headlong zeal to play all the notes perfectly, other aspects of music can suffer, with nuance, dynamics and tone color neglected. I remember reading a book on the interpretation of music. The author was a noted scholar. He warned his readers not to delude themselves. Dynamics, when used wisely, create sensational musical effects. I urge readers to listen to the great cellist of yesteryear, Ennio Bolognini, playing his own composition the Echo Serenade. His dynamics were achieved through genuine artistry. They were not done by somebody twisting the knobs in the control booth. I heard him play this piece in person when I studied with him. As a final thought, I also realize how lucky we are to have the Piedmont Center for the Arts. There is no better place than the PCA to enjoy chamber music. In general, it would be nice to see young folks attending concerts. Do teachers in the schools require their music students to attend concerts? In my day, students were required to attend concerts. They were also encouraged to write reviews. It was part of their grade. A city of culture An orchestra legitimizes a city. Piedmont has its own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which will present a gala concert this Sunday, November 6 at 4 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As one of the performers, I invite all of you to attend… And please bring the kids. A generous underwriter stepped forward recently, and the concert will be free for everyone.

The featured soloist is pianist Aaron Diehl, who appeared in the New York Philharmonic’s online presentation of “An All-American Program” and in selections from the chamber-orchestra version of the Zodiac Suite. John Kendall Bailey will give a pre-concert talk from the stage beginning at 7 p.m. The concert begins at 8 p.m. For tickets, visit https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/event/ psalms-by-bernstein/. Living the good life By Joseph Gold Revelations of the liquid kind. Are you a gourmet or a gourmand? Most of us enjoy good food. That is the gourmand in us. But there is more to life than just eating well. This was clearly demonstrated to me a few years ago when I was invited to a banquet. It was a multi-course affair with every plate selected with great care. Each course was paired with a wine designed to bring out the best. All of the diners were advised to take a bite of the first course and then sip the accompanying wine. The flavor literally exploded in our mouths. What a revelation it was. Just recently I attended a class on the enjoyment of wine. The expert told us that it is better not to drink the wine but to enjoy it in other ways. He suggested that we conjure up a vocabulary to describe the wines. In wine appreciation the nose is the best sense we have, followed by the taste buds. Our instructor told us that there are no taste buds in the throat, so don’t swallow the wine. The eyes play an important part also. The first wine we sampled was from Hungary. The person next to me was a Hungarian, who observed that the wine had the color of Tokay. Soon after that, our instructor said the very same thing. The next thing we were told to do was to use our nose to breathe the wine in deeply and conjure up descriptive words. My uneducated pallet sensed citrus overtones. I was right. Our instructor used the word “linden” which is the German word for lime. A person nearby was a recovering alcoholic, but he was an enthusiastic participant. He sniffed every wine, but the wine did not touch his lips… Ever. A sensational discovery Almost 100 years ago the tomb of king Tut was discovered by Howard Carter. The date was November 4, 1922. The discovery spawned every sort of Egyptology. You can get yourself in the mood by listening to Ballet Egyptian by Luigini, selections from Aida, or Africa by St-Saens. Chamber music at Piedmont Center for the Arts The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco presented its 10th anniversary concert in Piedmont on Sunday afternoon. They showcased one of the pieces they played in their very first concert in 2012, the monumental Beethoven String Quartet Op. 132. But there were other musical pieces to admire. To begin the concert, the quartet performed a new composition by Carolyn Shaw entitled Valencia. The composer has a unique way of looking at things. Her composition was about the Valencia orange not the city in Spain. It embraced every aspect of the orange from planting to eating. It was colorful, flavorful, piquant, with zesty eruptions of juicy chords. There was even a dark section where I envisioned a chef broiling the orange. Mozart’s unique “Dissonant” quartet came next, and then the Beethoven quartet brought the concert to a conclusion. The chamber music Society of San Francisco plays with incredible technical bravado. It can become intoxicating in its perfection. Their ensemble is tight. The word “perfection” comes to mind as I listened in amazement. But then I began to think that in the headlong zeal to play all the notes perfectly, other aspects of music can suffer, with nuance, dynamics and tone color neglected. I remember reading a book on the interpretation of music. The author was a noted scholar. He warned his readers not to delude themselves. Dynamics, when used wisely, create sensational musical effects. I urge readers to listen to the great cellist of yesteryear, Ennio Bolognini, playing his own composition the Echo Serenade. His dynamics were achieved through genuine artistry. They were not done by somebody twisting the knobs in the control booth. I heard him play this piece in person when I studied with him. As a final thought, I also realize how lucky we are to have the Piedmont Center for the Arts. There is no better place than the PCA to enjoy chamber music. In general, it would be nice to see young folks attending concerts. Do teachers in the schools require their music students to attend concerts? In my day, students were required to attend concerts. They were also encouraged to write reviews. It was part of their grade. A city of culture An orchestra legitimizes a city. Piedmont has its own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which will present a gala concert this Sunday, November 6 at 4 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As one of the performers, I invite all of you to attend… And please bring the kids. A generous underwriter stepped forward recently, and the concert will be free for everyone. Oakland Symphony’s guest soloist on November 4 is pianist Aaron Diehl. A Christmas Carol returns to ACT on November 30 By Allyson Aleksey As reliable as the swallows returning each year to San Juan Capistrano, A Christmas Carol returns to San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater (ACT) with performances from November 30 to December 24. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dickens’ novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly 100 years. ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo, with music scored by Karl Lundenberg and choregraphy by Val Caniparoli. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades. Performances will take place at its theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco, recently named the Toni Rembe Theater. For tickets. visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/202223-season/christmas-carol/. Cast members of a past production of A Christmas Carol by American Conservatory Theatre. articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers will be celebrating its 108th anniversary with an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, opening Sunday, November 6. An artists’ reception will be held on Friday November 11, from 6:00 to 9:00 p.m. The exhibition features the work of more than 80 printmakers and highlights a wide variety of printmaking techniques, including serigraphs, monotypes, lithographs, etchings, woodcuts, and aquatints. The talented artists represent CSP members from throughout California. Some examples of the myriad of forms of printmaking include Oakland artist Luz Marina Ruiz, whose work is a handmade artist Tunnel Book. Within the three-dimensional work, Luz incorporates linocuts embellished with watercolor and gouache on BFK paper. Another artist, Toru Sugita from Albany, depicts the changing or transitional monuments of the Bay Area using his own photographs and sketches of his surroundings to capture these spaces and textures through screen printing. Alicia Persaud, from Santa Cruz, also creates work influenced by their environment. In her work on display she uses photo-intaglio with digital chine collé, to generate both sharp and blurred qualities layered together. Toru Sugita, Bridge Composit, Screen print, 11.5” x 17”, 2022 She describes her process as, “depicting movement and motion of my memories both aesthetically through the imagery as well as emotionally through the physicality of the photo intaglio-process itself, highlighting how memories often blend together and change over time”. Some printmakers like Katherine Levin Lau from San Jose create images by hand painting on a zinc plate and then running the piece through the press many times. In Katherine’s detailed and dreamy scenes of nature, the original paintings are monochromatic. She enhances them with color layers using viscosity techniques. A final example of the breadth of techniques that will be on view is a work from Los Angeles artist Roxanne Sexauer, who utilizes a combination of printing methods including relief, monoserigraph, stencil, and chine collé to develop rich layers of abstract images. Only a small sampling of the unique work has been described here. To see these and more than 80 other visually compelling prints, visit the display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonta Avenue. The exhibit will be on view Saturdays and Sundays from November 6 to November 27. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. For more information visit http://www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org/ or http://www.caprintmakers.org/.

Sylvia Brownrigg reads in front of imagery by Danae Mattes and Christel Dillbohner from the performance “Lightfast” at the Museum of Craft and Design in San Francisco. Cellist Monica Scott was the instrumentalist in this four-woman collaboration of multimedia performance and installation. Review by Jaime Robles Theater, with its melding of text, performance, music and dance, has long depended on collaboration, but among artists working in forms that are most often practiced separately and individually collaboration takes on a very personal dimension. And its relationship to the audience is also less formal and more approachable. Lightfast, a multimedia performance and installation at the wonderful Museum of Design and Art in San Francisco, explores the realm of collaboration between artists. The result was a performance that was intimate, multi-faceted and elegant. The four artists behind Lightfast are novelist and short story writer Sylvia Brownrigg, cellist Monica Scott, and visual artists Christel Dillbohner and Danae Mattes. Beginning in 2020 the four women began conversing and collecting the images – musical, verbal and visual – that they ultimately shaped into last weekend’s performance. The program to Lightfast lists the elements of the piece, which can be thought of as movements, or facets, of a coherent and blended portrait of the world shared by the four collaborators. The space Lightfast inhabited at the museum was a large rectangular room, with chairs for an audience of about 50 viewers placed in rows along one of the long sides of the room. Two sets of deciduous tree branches were suspended in diagonal corners of the room. The branches looked like they had been dipped in thick pale gray paint. The lights above them caused their shadows to fall in soft blurry pink and greenish traceries across the white walls. The performance began with the entrance of the cellist. Scott placed herself and her instrument inside a gauzy cone of white mosquito netting that cascaded to the floor in front and to the right of the wall to the audience’s left. As the deep sounds of the cello resonated in the gallery space, a film of waves on sand plays was projected across most of the wall behind her. These were not the large rolling waves of surf, but waves after they have broken and become a simpler sheen of water over sand, expanding and retracting like breath. This imagery assembled by visual artists Dillbohner and Mattes was overlaid with other less distinct patterns of grays and lights, giving the play of water an abstract and dreamlike quality. Within the pale netting, the cellist became a ghostly figure, blurred and indistinct like the light on the waves. Like most of the imagery used in Lightfast, the colors used in the two films and a later series of projected stills were muted, as close to grays as possible. The deep sounds of the cello anchored the figure and images. Later in the performance the images shifted to another wall, the waves replaced by organic forms that were familiar but not clearly recognizable. Trees, grasses. A woman’s body appearing, disappearing, and reappearing seemed to float among the layered images. No story was told, instead emotions were evoked. There was no need for explanation of the beauty of the imagery or the sounds of the music. Instead, they formed an environment that was tender, meditative and nuanced. Into this shadowy and palely abstract world walked writer Brownrigg. In four monologues spaced in between shifting abstractions of music and image, she talked about the mysteries of family and the life on our green and blue planet. She talked about light and dark and silence: “It is not that the shadow knows, it is that the shadow speaks.” And finally, she talked about following a path, a trail where children, adults and elders walk, through a forest, across dry river bed of leaves, accompanied by the music of heat and insects. The museum’s space favored the cello over the spoken voice, but even so, the human voice has a music of its own, its words composed of a palette of sounds that, like the projected images, is subtle and serene. All performance is ephemeral, disappearing even as we watch. However, Lightfast has been recreated in book form, both as a large-format artists’ book and as a chapbook. Videos from the performance can be found on YouTube at https://m.youtube. com/playlist?list=PLHvdJYFqI- 4Ve3kLVy3Jo48GAjq6bqRYnj

articles.text: Visit the Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside throughout the month to see the 16-acre estate illuminated for the holidays. The non-profit and historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. An impressive myriad of decorations and over a dozen festooned Christmas trees enhances the estate’s historic and renowned elegance. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. Last year Filoli installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in the early to mid- 1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission provides access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more about “Holidays at Filoli” and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/. Filoli House and Garden will begin its holiday festivities on November 19.

articles.text: Members of the Cancer League, Inc. gathered at the home of Lisa Settlemier, its president, to assemble invitations for the 49th annual Holly Ball celebration on December 2. The Cancer League, a local nonprofit that funds groundbreaking research in cancer’s early stages, has announced details for the 49th annual Holly Ball, its largest annual fundraising event. This year’s Holly Ball will be on December 2 at Claremont Country Club and will have a Scottish theme. Holly Ball: Great Scot! will whisk guests away to the Scottish Highlands for a night of, eating, drinking, dancing and general merriment. Guests are encouraged to come dressed in their finest Highland formal attire, including kilts and tartan. The black-tie event commences with a cocktail reception, where guests will meander through an enchanted forest followed by a dinner in a Scottish castle. Entertainment includes Scottish Fiddlers, Highland dancers, and a Bagpipe serenade. The night would not be complete without a live auction, raisethe-paddle, a raffle and dancing into the night. “This year we are particularly excited about our live auction prizes,” said Brooke Wall and Rebecca Heywood, Holly Ball co-chairs. “We have a pair of fullbody health scans from Prenuvo, a shooting and dinner experience for 10 at Wing & Barrel Ranch, an exciting golf vacation in the Scottish Highlands, and much more.” Individual tickets for the event are $425, and sponsorship at any level is welcome. Sponsors at the $1,500 level and above will be invited to the Sponsor Party on November 9. This year’s sponsors include John Muir Health/UCSF Health, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, the David & Susan Martin Foundation, Oakland KIA, and Gary Kovacs, and Rebecca & John Carlo Heywood.
