articles.text: Costieres de Nimes is a wine growing region between the ancient city of Nimes and the western Rhone delta. Formerly part of the Languedoc region of France it is now considered part of the southern Rhone family of wines. Wines from the region have been produced for over 2,000 years, and were consumed by the Greeks in pre-Roman times, making it one of the oldest vineyards in Europe. The area was settled by veterans of Julius Caesar’s campaigns in Egypt, and bottles of Costieres de Nimes bear the symbol of the Roman settlement of Nimes, a crocodile chained to a palm tree. The soil is a mixture of round river rocks similar to Chateauneuf du Pape and sandy alluvial soil and red shale. The climate is Mediterranean, like that of the Rhone valley, but is characterized by its proximity to the coast and sea breezes. The vast majority of wines that are produced are red from Syrah, Mourvedre, Grenache, Carignan, and Cinsault. The white wines are made from Bourboulenc, Clairette Blanc, Grenache Blanc and Roussanne. Some refreshing Rose wines are also produced. The Costieres de Nimes is a region that is transitioning from mainly a producer of low-priced bulk wines to a source of genuinely characterful, well-made wines. One of the things I like about the region is that unlike other regions, the prices have not skyrocketed, and the wines often represent great values. For more information on where you can access Costieres de Nimes wines contact Marion Helluy of Colangelo and Partners at mhelluy@ colangelopr.com. • 2021 Mas Carlot “L’irresistible” A pale pink rose made from mostly Grenache with a touch of Mourvedre. It gives up lots of juicy peach, citrus and pineapple in its clean, quaffable and delicious profile. This is the perfect picnic wine, and as the name suggests, would be pretty irresistible on a warm day. • 2019 Chateau Grand Escalion “Safranee” Operated by the Maison Gabriel Meffe, the is vineyard is sustainably farmed on ancient marl soil. The cuvee is 75% Syrah and 25% Grenache. Offering big, bright berry fruits, pepper, olive and hints of meatiness, it is a medium-bodied, elegant and rock-solid Cotes du Rhone style wine that has tons of character. A perfect companion to grilled burgers or ribs. • 2021 Chateau Mourgues du Gres “Galets Dores” This delightfully refreshing white wine is made from Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Marsanne and Viognier – quite a vinifera cast. It has loads of tropical fruits, pineapple and floral notes in its medium-bodied, thrillingly pure crisp and lengthy personality While it doesn’t skimp on texture, it has beautifully integrated acidity and will be versatile on the dinner table. I’d drink it over the coming year or two but wouldn’t be surprised to see it drink well longer. • 2020 Mas des Bressades “Cuvee Tradition” This wine is a 50/50 blend of Syrah and Grenache from one of the more famous producers in the region. It presents gorgeous aromas of plum, blackberry, crushed rocks, pepper and violets win a medium to full-bodied, fresh, focused, impeccably balanced style. I love its fruit and this rocking effort will drink nicely in its youth and keep through 2028. Like the other three wines, this wine offers great value to the consumer.

articles.text: In the last couple of years, police departments across the country have been in the news. Tensions have risen, and many departments have had challenges connecting with their communities in a positive way. Social distancing has made those connections even more difficult. Across that backdrop, Piedmont Police has restarted their Exploring program, Post 911. Open to young men and women ages 14-20, Exploring helps youth learn about law enforcement as a potential career. In the case of Post 911, youth receive training in law enforcement policy and procedures, tactical and physical training, and forensics. They also learn life skills and career development that are transferable across career fields- including team building, communication, character education, and leadership. “There are a lot of controversial thoughts around law enforcement,” said Explorer Douglas Chu. “I wanted to learn more and get a different perspective.” “I’m interested in law enforcement. This gives me a chance to learn more about it,” said Explorer William Tretola. Exploring is also a lot of fun and provides opportunities for local and national competitions. “We’re looking forward to the competitions” said several of the Explorers. The Scouts have been to the national Law Enforcement Competition in Chandler, Arizona six times. It usually happens in February, and they’re preparing for a return to the event in 2024. In the meantime, they will prepare for regional competitions in CaliExplorer Lucas Chau practices cuffing Officer David Cutler with Explorer William Tretola as backup. Sgt. Casalnuovo gives instructions to Explorer Douglas Chu before starting the scenario practice. Explorer William Tretola assesses the situation at the beginning of the scenario practice. fornia. Competitions can include different scenarios such as hostage negotiation and building searches, as well as marksmanship. Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo serves as one of the advisors for the Post, along with Officers David Cutler and Hugo Diaz. “My favorite thing about this program is the camaraderie that builds among the participants,” said Casalnuovo. “Kids from all walks of life who might not otherwise hang out together develop really great bonds.” “The opportunity to be a mentor to youth in our community is important to me. I had a lot of great mentors as I was growing up, and this is my way of giving back,” added Officer Cutler. At a recent meeting, Explorers walked through a felony stop scenario. With the advisors, they discussed how to approach a suspect, how to communicate with them and with each other, and how to keep the situation from escalating. Then they walked through a mock scenario. Officer Cutler served as a mock suspect (who was remarkably helpful for someone afoul of the law), while Sergeant Casalnuovo provided feedback from the side. “Exploring is an important program,” said Piedmont Scout Executive Kate Benson. “While it carries the character development that is central to all Scouting programs, Exploring is unique in how it prepares youth for different career paths. Youth will develop a lot of transferable skills, but more importantly they’ll get a jump start if they find that a given field is a great fit. We are proud to partner with the Piedmont Police Department and of the leadership they provide to this program.” Interested in Exploring? articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake – a Fall classic. • • Persimmon trees are very common in Bay Area backyards. I’m fortunate to have neighbors on two sides with persimmon trees. One is the Fuyu variety, round and squat, best eaten crunchy like an apple and usually raw as well. The other is the Hachiya variety that is oblong with a pointy bottom and must be ripened until it is very soft and squishy. The soft pulp from the Hachiya variety is what is typically used in baking. Eaten raw they are a dessert in themselves with a pudding-like texture. Make the spice blend ahead for the streusel topping the cake batter. There will be a bit extra to add it to either the streusel or cake to use all of it. Substituting a ready-made pumpkin pie spice works too. • • • • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 2 cups all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon baking powder 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend 1/4 teaspoon sea salt INSTRUCTIONS Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake Adapted from Gemma Stafford’s Apple Snack Cake Makes one 8-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the spice blend: • 1-1/2 teaspoons cinnamon, suggest a “baker’s variety” for robust flavor • 3/4 teaspoon nutmeg, freshly ground is best • 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger • 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice • 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves • Pinch of freshly ground black pepper For the streusel topping: • 1/2 cup walnuts, chopped to about 1/4” pieces • 1/3 cup old-fashioned oats • 1/3 cup brown sugar • 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend • 2 tablespoons butter, melted For the persimmon cake: • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp, from 2 – 3 very ripe Hachiya persimmons, slightly drained of their liquid • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin (“fruity” or “grassy “profile, but try a “peppery” one too) • 2 teaspoons apple cider vinegar Place an oven rack in the center position of the oven. Preheat to 350° F. Line an 8-inch square pan with baking parchment, covering up the sides with some extra above the rim to lift out the cake when ready. Set aside. For the spice blend: Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Set aside. For the streusel topping: Combine the oats, brown sugar, walnuts, and spice blend in a small bowl. Add the melted butter and stir to combine. Set aside. For the persimmon cake: Whisk together the all-purpose flour, baking soda, baking powder, spice blend and salt in a medium bowl. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, beat the eggs and granulated sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, using an electric hand-held mixer, or a stand mixer with the paddle attachment. This will take 3–5 minutes. Beat in the melted butter, olive oil, apple cider vinegar and vanilla. Slowly add the persimmon pulp and mix well. Add in the flour mixture and mix on low speed. Use a spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl to finish incorporating the dry ingredients into the wet mixture, taking care to not overbeat the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Sprinkle on the streusel topping evenly, making sure to get to the edges and corners of the pan. Bake for 30–35 minutes or until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Rest the cake in the pan for at least 20 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, November 2, 2022 It’s Fall – time for fresh persimmon coffee cake Photo by Deborah Quok Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake – a Fall classic. By Deborah Quok • • Persimmon trees are very common in Bay Area backyards. I’m fortunate to have neighbors on two sides with persimmon trees. One is the Fuyu variety, round and squat, best eaten crunchy like an apple and usually raw as well. The other is the Hachiya variety that is oblong with a pointy bottom and must be ripened until it is very soft and squishy. The soft pulp from the Hachiya variety is what is typically used in baking. Eaten raw they are a dessert in themselves with a pudding-like texture. Make the spice blend ahead for the streusel topping the cake batter. There will be a bit extra to add it to either the streusel or cake to use all of it. Substituting a ready-made pumpkin pie spice works too. • • • • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 2 cups all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon baking powder 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend 1/4 teaspoon sea salt INSTRUCTIONS Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake Adapted from Gemma Stafford’s Apple Snack Cake Makes one 8-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the spice blend: • 1-1/2 teaspoons cinnamon, suggest a “baker’s variety” for robust flavor • 3/4 teaspoon nutmeg, freshly ground is best • 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger • 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice • 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves • Pinch of freshly ground black pepper For the streusel topping: • 1/2 cup walnuts, chopped to about 1/4” pieces • 1/3 cup old-fashioned oats • 1/3 cup brown sugar • 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend • 2 tablespoons butter, melted For the persimmon cake: • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp, from 2 – 3 very ripe Hachiya persimmons, slightly drained of their liquid • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin (“fruity” or “grassy “profile, but try a “peppery” one too) • 2 teaspoons apple cider vinegar Place an oven rack in the center position of the oven. Preheat to 350° F. Line an 8-inch square pan with baking parchment, covering up the sides with some extra above the rim to lift out the cake when ready. Set aside. For the spice blend: Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Set aside. For the streusel topping: Combine the oats, brown sugar, walnuts, and spice blend in a small bowl. Add the melted butter and stir to combine. Set aside. For the persimmon cake: Whisk together the all-purpose flour, baking soda, baking powder, spice blend and salt in a medium bowl. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, beat the eggs and granulated sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, using an electric hand-held mixer, or a stand mixer with the paddle attachment. This will take 3–5 minutes. Beat in the melted butter, olive oil, apple cider vinegar and vanilla. Slowly add the persimmon pulp and mix well. Add in the flour mixture and mix on low speed. Use a spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl to finish incorporating the dry ingredients into the wet mixture, taking care to not overbeat the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Sprinkle on the streusel topping evenly, making sure to get to the edges and corners of the pan. Bake for 30–35 minutes or until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Rest the cake in the pan for at least 20 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool. Serve slightly warm or at room temperature. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Post 911: Piedmont Scouts thrive in police Explorer unit By Kate Benson In the last couple of years, police departments across the country have been in the news. Tensions have risen, and many departments have had challenges connecting with their communities in a positive way. Social distancing has made those connections even more difficult. Across that backdrop, Piedmont Police has restarted their Exploring program, Post 911. Open to young men and women ages 14-20, Exploring helps youth learn about law enforcement as a potential career. In the case of Post 911, youth receive training in law enforcement policy and procedures, tactical and physical training, and forensics. They also learn life skills and career development that are transferable across career fields- including team building, communication, character education, and leadership. “There are a lot of controversial thoughts around law enforcement,” said Explorer Douglas Chu. “I wanted to learn more and get a different perspective.” “I’m interested in law enforcement. This gives me a chance to learn more about it,” said Explorer William Tretola. Exploring is also a lot of fun and provides opportunities for local and national competitions. “We’re looking forward to the competitions” said several of the Explorers. The Scouts have been to the national Law Enforcement Competition in Chandler, Arizona six times. It usually happens in February, and they’re preparing for a return to the event in 2024. In the meantime, they will prepare for regional competitions in CaliExplorer Lucas Chau practices cuffing Officer David Cutler with Explorer William Tretola as backup. Sgt. Casalnuovo gives instructions to Explorer Douglas Chu before starting the scenario practice. Explorer William Tretola assesses the situation at the beginning of the scenario practice. fornia. Competitions can include different scenarios such as hostage negotiation and building searches, as well as marksmanship. Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo serves as one of the advisors for the Post, along with Officers David Cutler and Hugo Diaz. “My favorite thing about this program is the camaraderie that builds among the participants,” said Casalnuovo. “Kids from all walks of life who might not otherwise hang out together develop really great bonds.” “The opportunity to be a mentor to youth in our community is important to me. I had a lot of great mentors as I was growing up, and this is my way of giving back,” added Officer Cutler. At a recent meeting, Explorers walked through a felony stop scenario. With the advisors, they discussed how to approach a suspect, how to communicate with them and with each other, and how to keep the situation from escalating. Then they walked through a mock scenario. Officer Cutler served as a mock suspect (who was remarkably helpful for someone afoul of the law), while Sergeant Casalnuovo provided feedback from the side. “Exploring is an important program,” said Piedmont Scout Executive Kate Benson. “While it carries the character development that is central to all Scouting programs, Exploring is unique in how it prepares youth for different career paths. Youth will develop a lot of transferable skills, but more importantly they’ll get a jump start if they find that a given field is a great fit. We are proud to partner with the Piedmont Police Department and of the leadership they provide to this program.” Interested in Exploring? articles.text: Spencer Strellis passed away at the age of 88 on October 19, 2022. Smart, funny, generous, and kind, Spencer and Judy, his wife of 48 years, moved to Piedmont in 1973. Almost immediately he set about championing community events and organizations. He was a fixture in Fourth of July parades and block parties. He taught wine-making classes through the Piedmont Adult School at their home for many years. Bottles of home vintages still line their wine cellar. Spencer was always quick to volunteer in support of his family. When his children Eric, Lauren, and Keith took an interest in judo, Spencer took to the mat himself, earning an honorary black belt and opening a dojo. Later, Spencer served as the President of the Piedmont Swim Club where his stepdaughter Anne Patterson launched a long and successful swimming career. He also coached his daughter Paisley’s softball teams. He delighted in entertaining friends and family, hosting many parties at their home on Bonita Avenue. He loved arts and was a longtime supporter of Berkeley Repertory Theater, American Conservatory Theater, the Oakland Symphony, and San Francisco Opera. He enjoyed reciting the poetry of Kipling, Wordsworth, and Robert Service, among others. Born in Chicago on January 10, 1934, the son of Milton and Billie Strellis, Spencer moved around the country and world for his father’s work as an Army Engineer, including attending high school on Guam. While studying History and Political Science at the University of Illinois at Champaign Urbana, he spent breaks visiting his parents in Morocco, Italy, and other farflung destinations. Spencer attended Berkeley Spencer Strellis Spencer Strellis with daughters Anne Patterson (left) and Paisley Strellis. Judy and Spencer Strellis. At age 25, Spencer Strellis received his first photo ID as a member of the Alameda County Public Defender’s office. Law (then Boalt Hall). He truly found his calling as a criminal defense attorney, beginning his career at the Alameda County Public Defender’s Office in 1959. In private practice, Spencer tried more than 300 felony cases before a jury, including defending members of the Free Speech Movement, the Black Panther Party, and Chinese American community leaders. However, most of his clients were not known to the public. He worked tirelessly to ensure they were given a fair trial. Some of his proudest legal accomplishments took place outside of the courtroom. In 1973, Spencer co-founded California Attorneys for Criminal Justice and served as a director for many years. Later Spencer co-founded the Criminal Courts Bar Association, which gave defense lawyers, District Attorneys, and judges a chance to connect outside of the courtroom. Spencer shared his expertise as a professor of criminal law and trial skills at Hastings College and the Oakland College of the Law. More recently, Spencer served as the 2004 President of the Alameda County Bar Association. In addition to his wife and children, Spencer is survived by nine grandchildren and countless friends and family members who will miss him dearly. A memorial will be held on Saturday, November 12 from 1-4 p.m. at the Colombo Club where he was a member for more than 30 years, The location is 5321 Claremont Ave, Oakland, CA 94618. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the American Parkinson Disease Association, the ACLU, or the Oakland Library.

articles.text: Editor: As mayor of the great city of Piedmont, I know first-hand what makes an outstanding public servant. It takes patience, intellect, devotion to the common good and a keen eye for details. Most importantly, a great public servant has vision for a better future. I am writing to strongly urge my fellow Piedmonters to vote for Councilmember Betsy Andersen for Piedmont City Council and Dr. Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College Trustee. Betsy Anderson is a joy to serve with on the Council. Her calm demeanor and skilled intellect – honed as a practicing attorney – results in Betsy’s best work. Her passionate commitment to good government, fiscal restraint and excellent city services preserves the best of our small town. And, Betsy is dedicated to making Piedmont cleaner and greener for future generations. She’s taken a lead on ensuring our city is walkable, bikeable, and ready for the transportation challenges of the 21st century. And it’s because of Betsy’s leadership that Piedmont will enjoy a state-of-the-art pool in the near future. For many similar reasons, I am offering my strong support to Dr. Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College District Trustee. Cindi is completing her first term on the college board, and she goes toe to toe with entrenched interests constantly to promote sound fiscal management in this sprawling – and critical – community college district. Many Piedmonters - kids, adults, seniors – benefit from community college access. Cindi Reiss’s commitment to excellence in financial leadership and thoughtful long-range planning, make her the stand-out candidate for this role. Please vote to reelect Betsy Andersen for Piedmont City Council and Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College District. –Teddy Gray King Mayor, City of Piedmont

articles.text: Editor: I write to endorse Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for Piedmont School Board. Put simply, both Ruchi and Lindsay have done their homework and demonstrated their commitment to serving the entire community. They have spoken and listened to the teachers, parents, students, administrators, and local organizations. During the Tri-School Parent Club School Board forum on October 25th, when asked about their qualifications, both Lindsay and Ruchi stated that they “show up.” Yes, they do show up. I am the mother of an autistic boy with an IEP at Beach. His brothers go to Wildwood. We are grateful for the special education resources at Beach, but we are deeply concerned about what lies ahead for our son when he will be in middle school and high school. Inclusion is extremely important to our family. Because special education, especially at the middle and high school levels, is extremely important not just to my family, but to so many other Piedmont families, I am proud to serve on the board of PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy, & Information in Special Education). PRAISE had a School Board Candidate forum on October 17. Twenty minutes before the forum, candidate Shirley Hooi emailed to say she would not be attending. Ruchi and Lindsay came prepared, and they were inspiring. I admit that only since the pandemic and schools closed did I realize how important it is to have people on the School Board with young school children. It is important to have people on the Board with diverse learners, and people who understand the importance of inclusion in our schools. As school board members, I believe that Ruchi and Lindsay will continue to show up and continue to thoughtfully engage with PRAISE and all of the other school district stakeholders who care so much about Piedmont’s amazing schools. articles.text: NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that at 5:30 p.m. on November 14, 2022, the Planning Commission will review an ordinance amending Chapter 17 (Planning and Land Use) of the City Code to conform the City’s regulations regarding Accessory Dwelling Units to new state laws and make a recommendation to the City Council. The ordinance also includes a new division 17.42 to address CA Assembly Bill 916, which requires ministerial review for the development of new bedrooms within existing residential units. NOTICE IS FURTHER GIVEN that at 6:00 p.m. on November 21, 2022, the City Council will consider the proposed ordinance and the recommendation of the Planning Commission and could approve the first reading of the ordinance. Background On January 1, 2022, new state laws come into effect which further limit a local jurisdiction’s ability to regulate Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). The provisions affected by the changes to state law include but are not limited to: street (front) yard setbacks, unit height limitations, approval of existing conditions inconsistent with current Building Code requirements, interior connections between a Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit and the Primary Dwelling Unit, and the separate conveyance of ADUs. City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. A staff report to the Planning Commission dated November 14, 2022, is provided on the website. It includes the proposed changes that will bring the City’s regulations for ADUs and additional bedrooms into compliance with the new state laws. The Planning Commission’s responsibility is to make a recommendation for consideration by the City Council, which is the decision-making body. The City Council staff report for this item will be posted on the City website no later than 12 noon on Friday, November 18, 2022. Public Engagement The opportunity for public input is available throughout this process. Interested members of the public are encouraged to attend the public meetings. Both the Planning Commission meeting on November 14, 2022, and the City Council meeting on November 21, 2022, will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and available through streaming video on the City’s web site at piedmont.ca.gov/. Written comments regarding the proposed ordinance may be sent to the City Council and Planning Commission via email to: citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov. Comments intended for the Planning Commission’s consideration should be submitted by 5 p.m., Thursday, November 10, 2022. To send comments via U.S. Mail, please use the following address: Piedmont City Council c/o City Clerk, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. If you have questions about the applications, please contact Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. A staff report to the Planning Commission dated November 14, 2022, is provided on the website. It includes the proposed changes that will bring the City’s regulations for ADUs and additional bedrooms into compliance with the new state laws. The Planning Commission’s responsibility is to make a recommendation for consideration by the City Council, which is the decision-making body. The City Council staff report for this item will be posted on the City website no later than 12 noon on Friday, November 18, 2022. Public Engagement The opportunity for public input is available throughout this process. Interested members of the public are encouraged to attend the public meetings. Both the Planning Commission meeting on November 14, 2022, and the City Council meeting on November 21, 2022, will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and available through streaming video on the City’s web site at piedmont.ca.gov/. Written comments regarding the proposed ordinance may be sent to the City Council and Planning Commission via email to: citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov. Comments intended for the Planning Commission’s consideration should be submitted by 5 p.m., Thursday, November 10, 2022. To send comments via U.S. Mail, please use the following address: Piedmont City Council c/o City Clerk, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. If you have questions about the applications, please contact Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. Any correspondence sent to the City will be considered a public record. John O.
